claim_checks.section: ## Summary
claim_checks.claim: RFC 10017 names three architectures for a browser app that uses OAuth and lists them in decreasing order of security: a BFF ..., a token-mediating backend ..., and a browser-based OAuth client that handles all of OAuth in the browser
claim_checks.page_says: Each of these architectural patterns offers a different trade-off between security and simplicity. The patterns in this section are presented in decreasing order of security.
claim_checks.note: Section 6 intro lists the three patterns with the same descriptions.

claim_checks.section: ## Summary
claim_checks.claim: None of the browser's persistent storage APIs (`localStorage`, `sessionStorage`, IndexedDB) can fully stop token exfiltration once attacker code runs in the app
claim_checks.page_says: none of these options can fully mitigate token exfiltration when the attacker can execute malicious code in the application's execution environment.
claim_checks.note: Section 8.5; the three APIs are named just before.

claim_checks.section: ## 1. Mental model > ### The problem
claim_checks.claim: A JSON Web Token (JWT) is "a string representing a set of claims as a JSON object that is encoded in a JWS or JWE", which lets the claims be signed or protected with a message authentication code (MAC) and/or encrypted
claim_checks.page_says: A string representing a set of claims as a JSON object that is encoded in a JWS or JWE, enabling the claims to be digitally signed or MACed and/or encrypted.

claim_checks.section: ## 1. Mental model > ### The thesis
claim_checks.claim: RFC 10017 says the BFF counters token theft by exposing no tokens to the browser app: "Even when the attacker gains full control over the application, there are simply no tokens to be stolen."
claim_checks.page_says: The BFF counters the first two attack scenarios by not exposing any tokens to the browser-based application.
claim_checks.note: The first two scenarios are the token theft scenarios; the quote follows on the same line.

claim_checks.section: ## 1. Mental model > ### The thesis
claim_checks.claim: RFC 7009 contrasts two token styles. An authorization server can revoke a handle-style access token, because the resource server relays each received token to it; for a self-contained token, "some (currently non-standardized) backend interaction ... may be used when immediate access token revocation is desired"
claim_checks.page_says: the authorization server is able to revoke an access token previously issued to a client when the resource server relays a received access token
claim_checks.note: Section 3 (Implementation Note) has both cases and the quoted text.

claim_checks.section: ## 1. Mental model > ### The thesis
claim_checks.claim: Its other design option is short-lived access tokens renewed with refresh tokens, which lets the authorization server limit how long a revoked access token stays in use
claim_checks.page_says: Another design alternative is to issue short-lived access tokens, which can be refreshed at any time using the corresponding refresh tokens.
claim_checks.note: Next sentence: allows the AS to impose a limit on the time revoked access tokens are in use.

claim_checks.section: ## 1. Mental model > ### Scope
claim_checks.claim: "Browser-based application" has RFC 10017's meaning: an application downloaded and executed in a web browser, usually written in JavaScript, also called a single-page application (SPA)
claim_checks.page_says: An application that is dynamically downloaded and executed in a web browser, usually written in JavaScript. Also sometimes referred to as a "single-page application" or "SPA".

claim_checks.section: ## 2. Concept architecture > ### Tokens
claim_checks.claim: Access token: "credentials used to access protected resources"; the token "may denote an identifier used to retrieve the authorization information or may self-contain the authorization information in a verifiable manner"
claim_checks.page_says: The token may denote an identifier used to retrieve the authorization information or may self-contain the authorization information in a verifiable manner
claim_checks.note: Section 1.4.

claim_checks.section: ## 2. Concept architecture > ### Tokens
claim_checks.claim: Refresh token: a credential used to obtain a new access token when the current one becomes invalid or expires; issuing one is optional for the authorization server, RFC 6749 says it denotes an identifier, and it is used only with authorization servers, never sent to resource servers
claim_checks.page_says: Unlike access tokens, refresh tokens are intended for use only with authorization servers and are never sent to resource servers.
claim_checks.note: Section 1.5 also has 'optional at the discretion of the authorization server' and 'denotes an identifier'.

claim_checks.section: ## 2. Concept architecture > ### Tokens
claim_checks.claim: Bearer token: the "bearer" type is used by simply including the access token string in the request, as in `Authorization: Bearer mF_9.B5f-4.1JqM`
claim_checks.page_says: the "bearer" token type defined in [RFC6750] is utilized by simply including the access token string in the request
claim_checks.note: Example header matches section 7.1.

claim_checks.section: ## 2. Concept architecture > ### Tokens
claim_checks.claim: In browser-based clients the refresh token is typically a bearer token too, unless the app explicitly uses Demonstrating Proof of Possession (DPoP, RFC 9449)
claim_checks.page_says: For browser-based clients, the refresh token is typically a bearer token unless the application explicitly uses DPoP [RFC9449].

claim_checks.section: ## 2. Concept architecture > ### Three architectures
claim_checks.claim: BFF: the backend acts as a confidential OAuth client, manages the access and refresh tokens in a cookie-based session so no token reaches the browser app, and forwards every request to the resource server with the right access token added
claim_checks.page_says: The BFF manages OAuth access and refresh tokens in the context of a cookie-based session, avoiding the direct exposure of any tokens to the browser-based application.
claim_checks.note: Section 6.1 lists all three responsibilities.

claim_checks.section: ## 2. Concept architecture > ### Three architectures
claim_checks.claim: Attacker script in the page can still send requests to the BFF from within the user's browser, but `HttpOnly` cookies stop it from reading the session state itself
claim_checks.page_says: Note that the use of HttpOnly cookies prevents the attacker from directly accessing the session state, which prevents the escalation from client hijacking to session hijacking.
claim_checks.note: Same paragraph: 'the attacker is able to send requests to the BFF from within the user's browser'.

claim_checks.section: ## 2. Concept architecture > ### Three architectures
claim_checks.claim: Token-mediating backend: the backend obtains the tokens as a confidential client and gives the browser app the access token ...; attacker script cannot abuse refresh tokens or obtain a fresh set of tokens, but it can steal the access token from client-side storage or request a fresh one from the backend
claim_checks.page_says: since the access token is directly exposed to the application, the attacker can steal the token from client-side storage
claim_checks.note: Section 6.2: 'for obtaining tokens as a confidential client'; same paragraph covers refresh tokens and requesting a fresh token from the backend.

claim_checks.section: ## 2. Concept architecture > ### Revocation building blocks
claim_checks.claim: Revocation endpoint (RFC 7009): lets a client invalidate its tokens if the end user logs out, changes identity, or uninstalls the application
claim_checks.page_says: This revocation mechanism allows a client to invalidate its tokens if the end-user logs out, changes identity, or uninstalls the respective application.

claim_checks.section: ## 2. Concept architecture > ### Revocation building blocks
claim_checks.claim: Sender-constrained token: an access token scoped to one sender, which must show knowledge of a secret before the resource server accepts it; RFC 9700 names two methods in use, mutual TLS certificate-bound tokens (RFC 8705, ...) and DPoP (RFC 9449, ... usable by public clients)
claim_checks.page_says: Two methods for sender-constrained access tokens using proof of possession have been defined by the OAuth working group and are in use in practice
claim_checks.note: Section 4.10.1 also has the fingerprint and 'DPoP can be used with public clients'.

claim_checks.section: ## 3. How it works > ### 3.1 Why a valid signature outlives a logout
claim_checks.claim: A stateless API trusts a JWT "because the signature checks out and the exp claim is in the future"; it never asks a database whether the session is still good, which is why the token cannot be taken back
claim_checks.page_says: Your API trusts it because the signature checks out and the exp claim is in the future — it never asks a database whether the session is still good.
claim_checks.note: Next sentence: 'It's also why you can't take the token back.' Rank 4 is allowed in role 3.

claim_checks.section: ## 3. How it works > ### 3.2 Revoking at the authorization server (RFC 7009)
claim_checks.claim: The authorization server validates the client credentials (for a confidential client), then checks that the token was issued to the client asking, and refuses the request if either check fails
claim_checks.page_says: The authorization server first validates the client credentials (in case of a confidential client) and then verifies whether the token was issued to the client making the revocation request.
claim_checks.note: 'If this validation fails, the request is refused'.

claim_checks.section: ## 3. How it works > ### 3.2 Revoking at the authorization server (RFC 7009)
claim_checks.claim: It invalidates the token immediately; in practice there can be a propagation delay in which some servers know and others do not, and clients must not use the token after an HTTP 200 response
claim_checks.page_says: clients must not try to use the token after receipt of an HTTP 200 response from the server.
claim_checks.note: Same paragraph: 'The invalidation takes place immediately' and the propagation delay.

claim_checks.section: ## 3. How it works > ### 3.2 Revoking at the authorization server (RFC 7009)
claim_checks.claim: Access tokens of the same grant: if the authorization server does not support access token revocation, they are not immediately invalidated when the matching refresh token is revoked
claim_checks.page_says: If the authorization server does not support access token revocation, access tokens will not be immediately invalidated when the corresponding refresh token is revoked.

claim_checks.section: ## 3. How it works > ### 3.3 Refresh token rotation and replay detection
claim_checks.claim: With rotation, the authorization server issues a new refresh token with every access token refresh response; the previous one is invalidated, but the server keeps the relationship between them
claim_checks.page_says: the authorization server issues a new refresh token with every access token refresh response. The previous refresh token is invalidated, but information about the relationship is retained
claim_checks.note: Section 4.14.2.

claim_checks.section: ## 3. How it works > ### 3.3 Refresh token rotation and replay detection
claim_checks.claim: Detection works when a stolen refresh token is used by both the attacker and the legitimate client: one of them presents an invalidated token, the server cannot tell which, and it revokes the active refresh token, which stops the attack at the cost of forcing the legitimate client to obtain a fresh grant
claim_checks.page_says: The authorization server cannot determine which party submitted the invalid refresh token, but it will revoke the active refresh token.
claim_checks.note: The condition (used by both) and the cost are in the same paragraph.

claim_checks.section: ## 3. How it works > ### 3.3 Refresh token rotation and replay detection
claim_checks.claim: With short-lived access tokens, the refresh exchange is also where revocation happens: it "means refusing to issue the next access token", at the refresh boundary instead of mid-token
claim_checks.page_says: Revocation then means refusing to issue the next access token: you revoke at the refresh boundary instead of mid-token.

claim_checks.section: ## 3. How it works > ### 3.4 The BFF session and its CSRF defense
claim_checks.claim: Session state. With a client-side session (...) used in a BFF, the cookie only serves to obtain the user's tokens, so all control and revocation follow from the tokens: it suffices to revoke the user's access token and/or refresh token, without invalidating the cookie-based session
claim_checks.page_says: It suffices to revoke the user's access token and/or refresh token to prevent ongoing access to protected resources, without the need to explicitly invalidate the cookie-based session.

claim_checks.section: ## 3. How it works > ### 3.4 The BFF session and its CSRF defense
claim_checks.claim: CSRF. Because the interactions between the app and the BFF rely on cookies, the BFF has to account for CSRF (...); the `SameSite=Strict` attribute ensures its cookies are included only on same-site requests
claim_checks.page_says: Configuring the cookies with the SameSite=Strict attribute (see Section 6.1.3.2) ensures that the BFF's cookies are only included on same-site requests
claim_checks.note: Section 6.1.3.3 also says the BFF 'is required to account for' CSRF.

claim_checks.section: ## 3. How it works > ### 3.4 The BFF session and its CSRF defense
claim_checks.claim: A custom request header closes the gap that CORS leaves for requests sent without a preflight: cross-origin requests that carry a custom header always need a preflight, which makes CORS an effective CSRF defense
claim_checks.page_says: Cross-origin requests with a custom request header always require a preflight, which makes CORS an effective CSRF defense.

claim_checks.section: ## 3. How it works > ### 3.5 Sender-constrained tokens in a browser
claim_checks.claim: The client has to prove possession of a private key to use the token, so a stolen token is not usable by itself; RFC 10017 says this shifts the challenge from storing the token securely to storing the private key securely
claim_checks.page_says: one could say that using sender-constrained tokens shifts the challenge of securely storing the token to securely storing the private key.

claim_checks.section: ## 3. How it works > ### 3.5 Sender-constrained tokens in a browser
claim_checks.claim: In a browser OAuth client using DPoP, the signing key is a non-extractable `CryptoKeyPair` stored in IndexedDB, which "effectively prevents scenarios where the XSS attacker exfiltrates the application's tokens"
claim_checks.page_says: (a non-extractable [CryptoKeyPair] is stored using [W3C.IndexedDB]). As a result, the use of DPoP effectively prevents scenarios where the XSS attacker exfiltrates the application's tokens

claim_checks.section: ## 3. How it works > ### 3.5 Sender-constrained tokens in a browser
claim_checks.claim: It does not stop the attacker from running a new flow to get fresh tokens; even when DPoP is mandatory, the attacker can bind the fresh tokens to a key pair under its own control
claim_checks.page_says: Even when DPoP is mandatory, the attacker can bind the fresh set of tokens to a key pair under their control

claim_checks.section: ## 3. How it works > ### 3.6 A `jti` denylist at the resource server
claim_checks.claim: A token consumer may keep a JWT denylist as a simple form of replay protection or "as a workaround for the “stateless session” invalidation problem"; OWASP's sketch keys it on the (`jti`, `iss`) pair, inserts each entry with the token's `exp`, and checks a token by looking up the same pair
claim_checks.page_says: This might be for example used a simple form of JWT replay protection or as a workaround for the “stateless session” invalidation problem.
claim_checks.note: The sketch shows deny_list.insert((jti, iss), exp) and deny_list.contains((jti, iss)). Rank 3 is allowed in role 3.

claim_checks.section: ## 3. How it works > ### 3.6 A `jti` denylist at the resource server
claim_checks.claim: Keying it on the raw JWT or its SHA-256 hash "is not safe": an attacker holding a revoked JWT may produce another representation that still passes signature verification, through non-strict JWT parsing or, for ECDSA (...) JWTs, signature malleability
claim_checks.page_says: Using the raw JWT or a secure hash of the JWT (SHA-256(token)) as the denylist key is not safe
claim_checks.note: Both causes are listed right after it; 'might be able to' matches 'may'.

claim_checks.section: ## 4. Worked examples > ### 4.1 Reading the RFC 7519 example token
claim_checks.claim: RFC 7519 §3.1 gives the header `{"typ":"JWT","alg":"HS256"}`, the claims `{"iss":"joe","exp":1300819380,"http://example.com/is_root":true}` and the complete token below
claim_checks.page_says: Concatenating these encoded parts in this order with period ('.') characters between the parts yields this complete JWT
claim_checks.note: The token in the probe, once the display line breaks are removed, matches all three parts in section 3.1.

claim_checks.section: ## 4. Worked examples > ### 4.1 Reading the RFC 7519 example token
claim_checks.claim: On Node 24.22.1 (image `node:24.22.1-alpine`, kernel `7.2.12-orbstack-00394-gbecdd6130068`), this probe decoded the header and claims with no key and printed `alg=HS256 iss=joe is_root=true` and `exp=2011-03-22T18:43:00.000Z expired=true`
claim_checks.page_says: stdout: alg=HS256 iss=joe is_root=true / exp=2011-03-22T18:43:00.000Z expired=true
claim_checks.note: The probe can fail: JSON.parse throws on a bad decode, and the expect line checks the decoded exp. It uses no key. The claim is worded as an observation, and the runtime and kernel match harness.json.

claim_checks.section: ## 4. Worked examples > ### 4.2 Revoking a refresh token (RFC 7009)
claim_checks.claim: The RFC's example request, and its rule that the server answers HTTP 200 whether the token was revoked or the client sent an invalid token
claim_checks.page_says: The authorization server responds with HTTP status code 200 if the token has been revoked successfully or if the client submitted an invalid token.
claim_checks.note: The example request matches section 2.1 byte for byte.

claim_checks.section: ## 4. Worked examples > ### 4.3 A refresh token lifetime that rotation cannot stretch (RFC 10017)
claim_checks.claim: A user authorizes an app, which gets a 10-minute access token and an 8-hour refresh token. After 10 minutes ... a new refresh token that lasts 7 hours 50 minutes; this repeats until 8 hours have passed, and then the refresh request fails and the app must start a new Authorization Code flow
claim_checks.page_says: The authorization server returns a new access token that lasts 10 minutes and a new refresh token that lasts 7 hours and 50 minutes.
claim_checks.note: The rest of the example is in section 6.3.2.3.

claim_checks.section: ## 4. Worked examples > ### 4.4 Okta: rotation and reuse detection
claim_checks.claim: Rotation is the default for SPAs when you create or edit one; if a used refresh token is presented again, Okta immediately invalidates the most recently issued refresh token and all access tokens issued since the user authenticated
claim_checks.page_says: Okta immediately invalidates the most recently issued refresh token and all access tokens issued since the user authenticated.
claim_checks.note: 'Rotating refresh token behavior is the default for SPAs when you create or edit a SPA.'

claim_checks.section: ## 4. Worked examples > ### 4.4 Okta: rotation and reuse detection
claim_checks.claim: The grace period, during which the previous token stays valid after rotation, defaults to 30 seconds and can be set from 0 through 60; in the app's `settings.oauthClient`, the `refresh_token` object takes a `rotation_type` of `ROTATE` or `STATIC` and a `leeway` of 0 through 60, as in ...
claim_checks.page_says: The default number of seconds for the Grace period for token rotation is set to 30 seconds. You can change the value to any number from 0 through 60 seconds.
claim_checks.note: The rotation_type and leeway values and the JSON example match.

claim_checks.section: ## 4. Worked examples > ### 4.4 Okta: rotation and reuse detection
claim_checks.claim: The refresh call is a form POST to `/oauth2/v1/token` with `grant_type=refresh_token`, `scope=offline_access%20openid` and the `refresh_token`; the example response carries `"token_type": "Bearer"` and `"expires_in": 3600`
claim_checks.page_says: To refresh your access token and an ID token, you send a token request with a grant_type of refresh_token.
claim_checks.note: The example uses http --form POST .../oauth2/v1/token and scope=offline_access%20openid; the response has token_type Bearer and expires_in 3600.

claim_checks.section: ## 4. Worked examples > ### 4.5 Duende.BFF: a server-side session behind one cookie
claim_checks.claim: The BFF 4.0 example of a host that stores the session server-side uses `ResponseType = "code"`, `SaveTokens = true` and the `offline_access` scope for refresh tokens, and sets the cookie to `SameSite=Lax` because its identity provider is on a different site; the comment says `Strict` would stop the cookie being sent after login, and recommends `Strict` when the identity provider is on the same site as the BFF
claim_checks.page_says: Recommendation: Set it to 'strict' if your IDP is on the same site as your BFF.
claim_checks.note: The 'BFF 4.0 and later' snippet has every value; the guide's host 'stores the session server-side'.

claim_checks.section: ## 4. Worked examples > ### 4.5 Duende.BFF: a server-side session behind one cookie
claim_checks.claim: The front end sends `X-CSRF: 1` on every request to a BFF API endpoint, or the BFF answers 401 Unauthorized; local API routes must be marked with `.AsBffApiEndpoint()`, without which the header is not enforced
claim_checks.page_says: Every request to a BFF API endpoint must include the X-CSRF: 1 header. Without it, the BFF will reject the request with 401 Unauthorized.
claim_checks.note: 'Always call .AsBffApiEndpoint() on your local API routes. Without it, the X-CSRF header is not enforced'.

claim_checks.section: ## 4. Worked examples > ### 4.6 dj-rest-auth: both JWTs in `HttpOnly` cookies
claim_checks.claim: These are the guide's settings from its step "Configure Django Settings", whose comment says `JWT_AUTH_SECURE` must be `True` in production
claim_checks.page_says: 'JWT_AUTH_SECURE': False, # True in production!
claim_checks.note: The REST_AUTH and SIMPLE_JWT values in the doc match step 2 exactly; the page also says 'Always set JWT_AUTH_SECURE = True in production'.

claim_checks.section: ## 4. Worked examples > ### 4.6 dj-rest-auth: both JWTs in `HttpOnly` cookies
claim_checks.claim: At login the API sets `HttpOnly` cookies for both tokens; when a request comes back 401 because the access cookie expired, the SPA calls `POST /token/refresh/` with the refresh cookie and receives a new access cookie
claim_checks.page_says: API-->>Browser: Set HttpOnly cookies for access and refresh ... SPA->>API: POST /token/refresh/ with refresh cookie
claim_checks.note: From the sequence diagram, which also has '401 Unauthorized' and 'Set new access cookie'.

claim_checks.section: ## 4. Worked examples > ### 4.6 dj-rest-auth: both JWTs in `HttpOnly` cookies
claim_checks.claim: The production example sets `JWT_AUTH_SECURE: True`, an access token lifetime of 5 minutes and a refresh token lifetime of 1 day, and the checklist asks for 5 to 15 minutes
claim_checks.page_says: Short access token lifetime (5-15 minutes)
claim_checks.note: The production settings.py has 'JWT_AUTH_SECURE': True, timedelta(minutes=5), timedelta(days=1).

claim_checks.section: ## 4. Worked examples > ### 4.6 dj-rest-auth: both JWTs in `HttpOnly` cookies
claim_checks.claim: With SimpleJWT's `token_blacklist` app installed, a user's refresh token is blacklisted at logout and cannot be reused
claim_checks.page_says: Now when users logout, their refresh token is blacklisted and cannot be reused.
claim_checks.note: The page's steps also set ROTATE_REFRESH_TOKENS and BLACKLIST_AFTER_ROTATION, which the doc's config block in 4.6 already includes, so the condition holds in context.

claim_checks.section: ## 4. Worked examples > ### 4.7 A denylist bypass through a re-encoded signature
claim_checks.claim: On Node 24.22.1 (...), the verifier written for this probe, which decodes the signature with `Buffer.from(s, 'base64url')` and compares bytes, accepted both the issued token and a copy whose last signature character differs in its two unused bits; the SHA-256-keyed list missed the copy and the (`jti`, `iss`)-keyed list caught it, printing `same-string=false both-verify=true` and `hash-denylist-blocks-variant=false jti-denylist-blocks-variant=true`
claim_checks.page_says: const variant = token.slice(0, -1) + A[A.indexOf(token.at(-1)) ^ 1]; stdout: same-string=false both-verify=true / hash-denylist-blocks-variant=false jti-denylist-blocks-variant=true
claim_checks.note: The probe itself is valid: it can fail (c.jti throws if the variant is rejected), runs Node 24.22.1 and backs the bypass, so that part is observed. But XOR with 1 flips only the lowest bit of the 6-bit character value. The copy therefore differs in one of its two unused bits, not in both as the claim says (and as the probe's own comment, 'Flip the 2 spare low bits', says). The number in the claim contradicts the code.

claim_checks.section: ## 5. Reference & invariants > ### JWT processing (RFC 7519)
claim_checks.claim: `exp`, `nbf`, `iat`: A JWT MUST NOT be accepted on or after `exp`, nor before `nbf`; implementers MAY allow a small leeway, usually no more than a few minutes, for clock skew; `iat` is the time of issue and can be used to determine the token's age; all are NumericDate values and OPTIONAL
claim_checks.page_says: Implementers MAY provide for some small leeway, usually no more than a few minutes, to account for clock skew.
claim_checks.note: Sections 4.1.4 to 4.1.6 have each part with the same modal verbs.

claim_checks.section: ## 5. Reference & invariants > ### JWT processing (RFC 7519)
claim_checks.claim: `aud`: Each principal intended to process the JWT MUST identify itself with a value in `aud`; when `aud` is present and the processor is not in it, the JWT MUST be rejected; the claim is OPTIONAL
claim_checks.page_says: If the principal processing the claim does not identify itself with a value in the "aud" claim when this claim is present, then the JWT MUST be rejected.

claim_checks.section: ## 5. Reference & invariants > ### JWT processing (RFC 7519)
claim_checks.claim: `jti`: The value MUST be assigned so that an accidental collision is negligibly likely, and with several issuers collisions MUST be prevented across issuers too; it "can be used to prevent the JWT from being replayed"; OPTIONAL
claim_checks.page_says: collisions MUST be prevented among values produced by different issuers as well. The "jti" claim can be used to prevent the JWT from being replayed.

claim_checks.section: ## 5. Reference & invariants > ### JWT processing (RFC 7519)
claim_checks.claim: Validation: If any validation step fails, the JWT MUST be rejected; which algorithms are acceptable is an application decision, and a JWT that validates with an unacceptable algorithm SHOULD be rejected
claim_checks.page_says: Even if a JWT can be successfully validated, unless the algorithms used in the JWT are acceptable to the application, it SHOULD reject the JWT.
claim_checks.note: Section 7.2 opens with 'If any of the listed steps fail, then the JWT MUST be rejected'.

claim_checks.section: ## 5. Reference & invariants > ### OAuth tokens (RFC 6749, updated by RFC 9700)
claim_checks.claim: Refresh token storage: MUST be kept confidential in transit and storage, shared only between the authorization server and its client, and sent only over TLS (...); the authorization server MUST maintain the binding between a refresh token and its client
claim_checks.page_says: Refresh tokens MUST be kept confidential in transit and storage, and shared only among the authorization server and the client to whom the refresh tokens were issued.
claim_checks.note: Section 10.4 also has the TLS MUST and the binding MUST.

claim_checks.section: ## 5. Reference & invariants > ### OAuth tokens (RFC 6749, updated by RFC 9700)
claim_checks.claim: New refresh token on refresh: The authorization server MAY issue one; the client MUST then discard the old refresh token, and the server MAY revoke it
claim_checks.page_says: The authorization server MAY issue a new refresh token, in which case the client MUST discard the old refresh token and replace it with the new refresh token.
claim_checks.note: Next sentence: the server MAY revoke the old one.

claim_checks.section: ## 5. Reference & invariants > ### OAuth tokens (RFC 6749, updated by RFC 9700)
claim_checks.claim: Sender-constraining: Authorization and resource servers SHOULD sender-constrain access tokens (mutual TLS or DPoP); refresh tokens for public clients MUST be sender-constrained or use refresh token rotation
claim_checks.page_says: Refresh tokens for public clients MUST be sender-constrained or use refresh token rotation as described in Section 4.14.
claim_checks.note: Section 2.2.1 has the SHOULD for access tokens, giving mTLS and DPoP as examples.

claim_checks.section: ## 5. Reference & invariants > ### OAuth tokens (RFC 6749, updated by RFC 9700)
claim_checks.claim: Audience: Access tokens SHOULD be audience-restricted to one resource server or a small set; a resource server MUST refuse a token not meant for it; the `aud` claim MAY carry the restriction
claim_checks.page_says: access tokens SHOULD be audience-restricted to a specific resource server or, if that is not feasible, to a small set of resource servers.
claim_checks.note: The doc drops the condition 'if that is not feasible'. RFC 9700 allows a small set only as a fallback, but the doc gives it as an equal choice. The MUST and MAY parts match.

claim_checks.section: ## 5. Reference & invariants > ### OAuth tokens (RFC 6749, updated by RFC 9700)
claim_checks.claim: Security events and idle refresh tokens: Authorization servers MAY revoke refresh tokens automatically on a password change or a logout at the authorization server; refresh tokens SHOULD expire after the client has been inactive for some time, a period the server chooses
claim_checks.page_says: Refresh tokens SHOULD expire if the client has been inactive for some time
claim_checks.note: The page has the MAY with both events as examples, and 'The expiration time is at the discretion of the authorization server'.

claim_checks.section: ## 5. Reference & invariants > ### Browser-based applications (RFC 10017)
claim_checks.claim: BFF cookies: MUST set `Secure`; MUST set `HttpOnly`; SHOULD set `SameSite=Strict`; SHOULD use `Path=/`; SHOULD NOT set `Domain`; SHOULD give the cookie name a prefix showing it was set over HTTP, for example `__Host-Http-` from the `[COOKIES]` reference, which is draft-ietf-httpbis-layered-cookies-02 (21 May 2026), an Internet-Draft marked work in progress
claim_checks.page_says: The BFF SHOULD start the name of its cookie with a prefix indicating the cookie was set via HTTP, for example, by using the __Host-Http- prefix defined in [COOKIES].
claim_checks.note: Each modal matches section 6.1.3.2. The [COOKIES] entry reads 'Work in Progress, Internet-Draft, draft-ietf-httpbis-layered-cookies-02, 21 May 2026'.

claim_checks.section: ## 5. Reference & invariants > ### Browser-based applications (RFC 10017)
claim_checks.claim: CSRF: The BFF MUST implement a proper CSRF defense; when it relies on CORS it SHOULD require a custom request header, and when it uses one it MUST ensure every incoming request carries that header
claim_checks.page_says: When this mechanism is used, the BFF MUST ensure that every incoming request carries this static header.
claim_checks.note: 'The BFF MUST implement a proper CSRF defense' and the SHOULD for the custom header are in section 6.1.3.3.

claim_checks.section: ## 5. Reference & invariants > ### Browser-based applications (RFC 10017)
claim_checks.claim: Refresh tokens issued to browser-based apps: Authorization servers MUST rotate refresh tokens on each use OR sender-constrain them; MUST set a maximum lifetime OR expire unused refresh tokens; MUST NOT let a rotated refresh token outlive the initial one when it has a preset expiry
claim_checks.page_says: MUST NOT, upon issuing a rotated refresh token, extend the lifetime of the new refresh token beyond the lifetime of the initial refresh token
claim_checks.note: All three items are in section 6.3.2.3 with the same modal verbs.

claim_checks.section: ## 5. Reference & invariants > ### Browser-based applications (RFC 10017)
claim_checks.claim: Logout: Authorization servers SHOULD link the refresh token's lifetime to the user's session at the authorization server, so logout invalidates the refresh tokens issued to browser-based apps
claim_checks.page_says: Authorization servers SHOULD link the lifetime of the refresh token to the user's authenticated session with the authorization server.

claim_checks.section: ## 5. Reference & invariants > ### Browser-based applications (RFC 10017)
claim_checks.claim: Script-set cookies: Storing a token in a cookie through the JavaScript Cookie API is NOT RECOMMENDED, because the browser also sends that cookie to the app's own server
claim_checks.page_says: Because of these unintentional side effects of using cookies for JavaScript-based storage, this practice is NOT RECOMMENDED.
claim_checks.note: Section 8.1 explains that the browser sends the cookie to the app's domain.

claim_checks.section: ## 5. Reference & invariants > ### Revocation endpoint (RFC 7009)
claim_checks.claim: Support and transport: Implementations MUST support revoking refresh tokens and SHOULD support revoking access tokens; revocation endpoint URLs MUST be HTTPS URLs
claim_checks.page_says: Implementations MUST support the revocation of refresh tokens and SHOULD support the revocation of access tokens
claim_checks.note: 'URLs for token revocation endpoints MUST be HTTPS URLs'.

claim_checks.section: ## 5. Reference & invariants > ### Revocation endpoint (RFC 7009)
claim_checks.claim: Cascade: Revoking a refresh token SHOULD also invalidate all access tokens of the same grant when the server supports access token revocation; revoking an access token MAY revoke its refresh token
claim_checks.page_says: If the token passed to the request is an access token, the server MAY revoke the respective refresh token as well.
claim_checks.note: The SHOULD for the refresh token case and its condition come just before.

claim_checks.section: ## 5. Reference & invariants > ### A library rule: jsonwebtoken (CVE-2022-23540)
claim_checks.claim: `jsonwebtoken` <= 8.5.1: Signature validation can be bypassed because `jwt.verify()` defaults to the `none` algorithm; an app is affected if all three hold: a token with no signature arrives, no algorithms are specified, and a falsy secret or key (`null`, `false`, `undefined`) is passed; 9.0.0 removes the default support for `none`, which must then be named in the options if needed
claim_checks.page_says: You will be affected if all the following are true in the jwt.verify() function:
claim_checks.note: The page lists the three conditions, the version <=8.5.1 and the 9.0.0 fix, and says 'you have to explicitly specify that in jwt.verify() options'. Rank 3 is allowed in role 5.

claim_checks.section: ## 6. Trade-offs, pitfalls & misconceptions > ### "Keep the token in memory and XSS cannot get it"
claim_checks.claim: The misconception: some SPA OAuth libraries keep the access token in memory and isolate the refresh token in a Web Worker, which looks hard to steal. A proof of concept that redefines `MessageChannel` intercepts each access token the Web Worker sends back, so the attacker steals access tokens for as long as the app runs in the user's browser
claim_checks.page_says: This attack scenario allows the attacker to steal access tokens as long as the application is running in the user’s browser.
claim_checks.note: Rank 6, and in role 6 only. The page describes the Web Worker option and the MessageChannel proof of concept.

claim_checks.section: ## 6. Trade-offs, pitfalls & misconceptions > ### "Keep the token in memory and XSS cannot get it"
claim_checks.claim: The author's advice is not to worry much about storage: in-memory or Web Worker storage "makes an attack harder, but it never solves the root problem" (XSS itself)
claim_checks.page_says: use in-memory storage or the Web Worker option. It makes an attack harder, but it never solves the root problem.
claim_checks.note: Under 'Step 1: don’t worry too much about storage'.

claim_checks.section: ## 6. Trade-offs, pitfalls & misconceptions > ### "Keep the token in memory and XSS cannot get it"
claim_checks.claim: Persistent theft: injected code that steals the latest tokens on a timer always holds the newest ones, which "already suffices to counter typical defenses against token theft, such as short lifetimes or refresh token rotation"; it can also make sure the app never uses the latest refresh token (...), so no reuse is ever detected
claim_checks.page_says: This slight variation in the attack scenario already suffices to counter typical defenses against token theft, such as short lifetimes or refresh token rotation.
claim_checks.note: Section 5.1.2 also has 'there will be no detectable refresh token reuse'.

claim_checks.section: ## 6. Trade-offs, pitfalls & misconceptions > ### "Keep the token in memory and XSS cannot get it"
claim_checks.claim: New tokens: attacker code can ignore stored tokens altogether, open a hidden iframe and run a silent Authorization Code flow on the user's existing authorization-server session, getting a new, independent access token; this relies on the authorization server supporting silent frame-based flows
claim_checks.page_says: the attacker can inject a hidden iframe and launch a silent Authorization Code flow. This silent flow will reuse the user's existing session with the authorization server

claim_checks.section: ## 6. Trade-offs, pitfalls & misconceptions > ### Rotation detects some theft, not all
claim_checks.claim: The vendor post says a replayed stale refresh token is the signal by which rotation detects theft
claim_checks.page_says: If a stale refresh token is replayed, that's a signal something is wrong
claim_checks.note: This records a disagreement. The doc puts the Rank 4 view in role 6 and sets it against the conditions in RFC 9700 and RFC 10017.

claim_checks.section: ## 6. Trade-offs, pitfalls & misconceptions > ### Short lifetimes versus a denylist
claim_checks.claim: With short access tokens, "instant" revocation really means "within one token lifetime", so the lifetime is a security-versus-latency choice
claim_checks.page_says: The tradeoff is that "instant" really means "within one token lifetime," so the TTL you choose is a direct security-versus-latency decision.

claim_checks.section: ## 6. Trade-offs, pitfalls & misconceptions > ### Short lifetimes versus a denylist
claim_checks.claim: A server-side denylist is precise, but every request then does a lookup, the database round-trip JWTs were adopted to avoid
claim_checks.page_says: now every request does a lookup, which is the database round-trip you adopted JWTs to avoid.

claim_checks.section: ## 6. Trade-offs, pitfalls & misconceptions > ### Short lifetimes versus a denylist
claim_checks.claim: Stateless JWT sessions: OWASP says JWT user sessions need a way to invalidate sessions, such as a deny list, after which they are no longer completely stateless, and suggests considering a plain session system
claim_checks.page_says: If your application implements such a deny list, user sessions won't be completely stateless anymore which might defeat the benefits of stateless sessions.

claim_checks.section: ## 6. Trade-offs, pitfalls & misconceptions > ### Sender-constrained tokens and XSS
claim_checks.claim: RFC 9700 says sender-constraining is undermined when an attacker gets both the token and the key material, in particular through cross-site scripting when the client runs in the browser
claim_checks.page_says: Note that the security of sender-constrained tokens is undermined when an attacker gets access to the token and the key material.
claim_checks.note: This records an apparent clash with RFC 10017 section 3.5, which the doc resolves as two conditions, each with its Rank 1 source.

claim_checks.section: ## 6. Trade-offs, pitfalls & misconceptions > ### Cookies: SameSite and Domain
claim_checks.claim: `SameSite=Strict` is adequate only if the BFF is never same-site with another app: `https://a.example.com` and `https://b.example.com` share the site `example.com`, so a subdomain takeover of `b.example.com` can enable CSRF against the BFF on `a.example.com`
claim_checks.page_says: This defense is adequate if the BFF is never considered to be same site with any other applications.
claim_checks.note: The same section has the a/b.example.com example.

claim_checks.section: ## 6. Trade-offs, pitfalls & misconceptions > ### Cookies: SameSite and Domain
claim_checks.claim: dj-rest-auth calls `Lax` its default and recommended value and says `Strict` "may break some flows", and documents `JWT_AUTH_COOKIE_DOMAIN: '.example.com'` to share cookies across subdomains
claim_checks.page_says: 'JWT_AUTH_SAMESITE': 'Lax', # Default, recommended
claim_checks.note: The table has 'Maximum security, may break some flows' for Strict, and the COOKIE_DOMAIN example is there. This records a disagreement with RFC 10017, which the doc settles in favour of Rank 1 for BFFs.

claim_checks.section: ## 6. Trade-offs, pitfalls & misconceptions > ### Cookies: SameSite and Domain
claim_checks.claim: Encrypting a client-side session cookie keeps the tokens out of plaintext on disk, but an attacker can still use the encrypted cookie in a session hijacking attack
claim_checks.page_says: Note that while encrypting the cookie contents prevents direct access to embedded tokens, it still allows the attacker to use the encrypted cookie in a session hijacking attack.

claim_checks.section: ## 6. Trade-offs, pitfalls & misconceptions > ### `alg: none` and algorithm confusion
claim_checks.claim: A verifier that reads the `alg` header to pick the algorithm lets the attacker choose how the signature is checked; some libraries treated `alg: none` tokens as validly signed, so anyone could create tokens with any payload
claim_checks.page_says: some libraries treated tokens signed with the none algorithm as a valid token with a verified signature.
claim_checks.note: The page also says 'we have to allow attackers to select which method we use to verify the signature'.

claim_checks.section: ## 6. Trade-offs, pitfalls & misconceptions > ### `alg: none` and algorithm confusion
claim_checks.claim: Algorithm confusion: a server expecting an RSA-signed token that receives an HMAC (...) one treats its RSA public key as the HMAC secret, so anyone with the public key can forge tokens that pass, provided the key string matches the server's exactly, format and line breaks included
claim_checks.page_says: The strings must match exactly for the attack to work -- exact same format, and no extra or missing line breaks.

claim_checks.section: ## 6. Trade-offs, pitfalls & misconceptions > ### `alg: none` and algorithm confusion
claim_checks.claim: The 2015 post says most implementations by then failed `none` tokens "if a secret key was provided"
claim_checks.page_says: Most (hopefully all?) implementations now have a basic check to prevent this attack: if a secret key was provided, then token verification will fail for tokens using the none algorithm.
claim_checks.note: The page's TL;DR reads 'Updated 2015-04-20' (the byline shows Aug 21, 2020). This records a disagreement with the advisory; the doc settles it in role 6.

claim_checks.section: ## 6. Trade-offs, pitfalls & misconceptions > ### Older text that a newer Rank 1 source replaces
claim_checks.claim: RFC 6749 says that, when client authentication is not possible, the authorization server SHOULD deploy other means to detect refresh token abuse, and gives rotation as something it "could employ"
claim_checks.page_says: When client authentication is not possible, the authorization server SHOULD deploy other means to detect refresh token abuse.
claim_checks.note: Next sentence: 'the authorization server could employ refresh token rotation'.

claim_checks.section: ## 6. Trade-offs, pitfalls & misconceptions > ### Older text that a newer Rank 1 source replaces
claim_checks.claim: RFC 9700 updates RFC 6749
claim_checks.page_says: Updates RFC 6749, RFC 6750, RFC 6819

claim_checks.section: ## 6. Trade-offs, pitfalls & misconceptions > ### Older text that a newer Rank 1 source replaces
claim_checks.claim: RFC 9700 says refresh tokens SHOULD expire after client inactivity (§5); for browser-based apps RFC 10017's MUST (cap the lifetime or expire unused tokens) governs, since RFC 10017 "expands on and further restricts various recommendations given in [RFC9700]"
claim_checks.page_says: This document expands on and further restricts various recommendations given in [RFC9700].
claim_checks.note: The MUST is in section 6.3.2.3 (see C57).

violations.section: ## 4. Worked examples > ### 4.7 A denylist bypass through a re-encoded signature
violations.evidence: C45: the claim says the copy's last signature character 'differs in its two unused bits', but probe-02 builds it with `A[A.indexOf(token.at(-1)) ^ 1]`, which flips only the lowest bit. The probe's comment 'Flip the 2 spare low bits' is wrong in the same way. The bypass result itself is observed.

violations.section: ## 5. Reference & invariants > ### OAuth tokens (RFC 6749, updated by RFC 9700)
violations.evidence: C53: 'audience-restricted to one resource server or a small set' drops RFC 9700's condition 'if that is not feasible' on the small-set option.

violations.section: ## 6. Trade-offs, pitfalls & misconceptions > ### `alg: none` and algorithm confusion; ## References
violations.evidence: The GitHub Advisory Database entry [^ghsa] is labelled Rank 2. It fits both official dataset (2) and curated reference (3), so the judge rates it 3. This breaks no quarantine (role 5 allows 1-4), and the role 6 ruling over the Rank 4 Auth0 post still holds.

Section 4.2 shows the request but no response. Sections 4.4 and 4.5 are mostly option ranges and setup rules rather than runs with outputs. Section 6 has no decision table for the doc's main 'Use this when' choice (BFF versus token-mediating versus browser-only, and where to store tokens).

patch_instructions.section: ## 4. Worked examples > ### 4.7 A denylist bypass through a re-encoded signature
patch_instructions.action: Option 1: in probe-02, change `A.indexOf(token.at(-1)) ^ 1` to `A.indexOf(token.at(-1)) ^ 3` so that both spare low bits flip, as the comment and the prose say, then rerun the probe and update the output line. Option 2: keep the code, change the comment to 'Flip the lowest spare bit', and reword the prose to 'a copy whose last signature character differs in the lower of its two unused bits'. Cite [^probe-02].

patch_instructions.section: ## 5. Reference & invariants > ### OAuth tokens (RFC 6749, updated by RFC 9700)
patch_instructions.action: In the Audience row, write: 'Access tokens SHOULD be audience-restricted to one resource server or, if that is not feasible, to a small set; ...' Keep [^rfc9700] (section 2.3: 'to a specific resource server or, if that is not feasible, to a small set of resource servers').

patch_instructions.section: ## 4. Worked examples > ### 4.2 Revoking a refresh token (RFC 7009); ## 6. Trade-offs, pitfalls & misconceptions
patch_instructions.action: Optional: in 4.2, add the response the rule implies, `HTTP/1.1 200 OK`, from RFC 7009 section 2.2 [^rfc7009].
